title: UK threatens visa bans for Eritrea over migrant return policy
description: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritreans from entering the UK if the east African country's government does not accept more
body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritreans from entering the UK if the east African country's government does not accept more returns of small boat migrants and foreign national offenders.From Thursday, Eritrean diplomats will face restrictions on their movement outside London. Fast-track visas will also be stopped for VIPs.Ministers have previously pressured other countries into accepting returns by threatening visa bans.Eritreans were the most common nationality among small boats migrants in the 12 months to June - accounting for 18% of arrivals, external, according to figures from the House of Commons Library.The Eritrean embassy in London has been contacted for comment."Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused," said Mahmood.She said she would not hesitate "to impose further measures on other countries refusing to co-operate".The UK government accused the Eritrean authorities of "abruptly" withdrawing co-operation earlier this year.The restrictions mean diplomats are banned from travelling 60km outside London without permission. The Home Office said this mirrored restrictions on British officials in Eritrea's capital Asmara.Earlier this year, the UK threatened bans against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of  Congo (DRC).Restrictions were announced against the DRC last year, but the Home Office said these have been lifted after co-operation on returns improved.Angola and Namibia both agreed changes before restrictions were introduced.When announcing changes to the UK's asylum system in November, Mahmood said visa penalties would be applied to countries that failed to co-operate with returns policies.Penalties included an "emergency brake" on visas for countries with high asylum claims until they take back citizens in the UK illegally.According to Home Office data, more than 20,400 people have arrived in the UK by small boats so far since the beginning of this year, down 40% from the same period last year.There were more than 40,600 returns and deportations from the UK from July 2025 to June this year - an 8% increase on the same period last year.Of those who had been returned, less than 6,000 has been convicted of a criminal offence.

schema.headline: UK threatens visa bans for Eritrea over migrant return policy

title: Brooklyn novelty shop reeling from 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
description: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.Inside,
body: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby in this Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000)."Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a  shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale. It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day."Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said. "It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit.The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird.She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier.But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises. One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy. For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise.Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days. Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here."I really like it here."

schema.headline: Brooklyn novelty shop reeling from 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird

title: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz after being hit by projectile, Singapore says
description: A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporea
body: A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporean authorities.All 21 crew members of GFS Pride were evacuated and no injuries were reported after the attack on Tuesday, which caused damage and a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said.Another Singapore-flagged container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage after being hit by a projectile on Wednesday but was able to reach a safe anchorage with all 22 crew, it added.Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the Strait of Hormuz.The Guards released photos that appeared to show a plume of black smoke rising from a container vessel that was still afloat but down by the stern. In other photos, dozens of containers and their contents could be seen floating in the water.The Hydrographer of Pakistan warned mariners that GFS Pride had sunk 4 nautical miles (7.4km) north-west of Ras al-Sheikh Masud in Oman's Musandam Peninsula.Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said that two unnamed container ships had reported being struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz between 16:40 and 17:00 GMT on Tuesday.Both vessels sustained minor damage and were able to continue their passages, it added.Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz - which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea - and elsewhere in the Middle East since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 106 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization.The Malta-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige, which was attacked near Oman on 4 March, is the only other vessel reported to have sunk in that time.However, maritime risk management group Vanguard said on Wednesday that the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt, according to Reuters news agency.One seafarer was killed when the Cape Dao's bridge and accommodation area were hit by an unknown projectile as it transited through the Strait of Hormuz, north-east of Khasab, Oman, on 23 September.The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.Last month, crude exports through the waterway rose to around 80% of pre-war levels of 16 million barrels per day (bpd) on average, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler, despite an increase in attacks on shipping.

schema.headline: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz after being hit by projectile, Singapore says

title: How data centres became the sleeper issue that could decide the US midterms
description: A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. ​​Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings wit
body: A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. ​​Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings with staff to track their impact and working on new legislation aimed at curbing their rapid expansion across the country."This happens sometimes, something starts slow and then it goes fast", the senior policy adviser to the Democratic senator told the BBC. The person spoke on condition of anonymity as they are not permitted to speak to the press.The 180-degree turn in this senator's attention was driven almost entirely by a growing wave of public backlash that has seen politicians across the country scramble to keep up. Public sentiment has turned against the expansion of data centres, the large warehouses that store processing power needed for internet activity.Packed with rows and rows of computer chips, sometimes seven-feet high, data centres have turned into more than infrastructure for the internet. They are now the physical embodiment of the recent and explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and the varied fears people associate with it. "I don't want to be the guinea pig for this," Indiana resident Angelita Soriano told the BBC. A backlash over data centres is another threat to the AI juggernautA new Amazon data centre is being built directly across the street from her home. When complete, the 26-building structure will take up more than a square mile in her neighbourhood and maintain 782 diesel-powered generators. Some data centres are even larger. In Ohio, a joint effort between OpenAI, Nvidia, SB Energy and the US Department of Energy is set to build a data centre complex that will stretch for roughly six square miles, the same size as most townships in the US.  There are about 3,000 data centres currently operating in the US, with that number potentially doubling in the next few years, according to a report by, external Pew Research Center.Data centres are built through very local rules and permits, meaning federal lawmakers like US senators have little say in the process.Yet, opposition has become so strong so quickly in the US that suddenly, politicians at all levels are now all but required to take a stand. "This isn't just an issue on the left, there is huge pushback among conservatives to data centres," Chloe Autio, an AI policy adviser, said. "Whoever articulates a clear position and sticks to it, in either party, really stands to benefit."Her analysis was echoed by the adviser to the US Senator working on data centre legislation."There is a clear policy need here that we're looking to fill," he said. "This is a major backlash across the country - constituents are seeing the impacts of data centres and they do not like them."That has put many on Capitol Hill - even Republicans - in direct conflict with President Donald Trump, who has championed the unrestrained growth of AI technology.Trump has dubbed the backlash to data centres a "sick conspiracy" and said people and towns working to keep the buildings out are "backwards and poor".His ire has been used as a boon to Democratic politicians looking to draw midterm votes from unhappy or undecided constituents.The BBC spoke to residents of Indiana, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon, all of whom have been organising locally against the development of data centres. They expressed concerns about many aspects of the buildings, including their size, construction and operational noise, their impact on air, water and energy resources, as well as the speed at which they seem to be approved by local authorities.During the first few months of this year, community groups organising against data centres more than doubled to 833, cropping up in almost every US state, according to research from Data Center Watch. The firm collects data for AI industry stakeholders and is part of an AI startup 10a Labs.Stephanie Maldonado, the political director of LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, referred to the push back against data centres as "a David and Goliath story" that began several years ago."People have been ready to put a stop to it," Maldonado added. "Now, people are angry."New national polling, external shows that AI regulation and data centres are among some of the top issues for voters this election cycle, behind the ongoing Iran War and various aspects of the economy.Proponents of building data centres often argue the projects will create more, and better paying, local jobs.Yet, recent research, external from Brookings Institution, a non-partisan policy research group, found that a new data centre creates between 100 and 200 local jobs, which is "fewer than industry advocates claim". The projects also have essentially no impact on local wages.Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs was one such proponent - until public pressure pushed her to the other side of the issue. In July, she enacted a three-year pause on any new tax break given to a company for a data centres project.Arizona is far from the only state to see politicians react to data centre backlash.Abdul El Sayed, a Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, made new rules and regulations for data centres a clear part of his successful primary campaign for Senate.In the race for governor of Georgia, a Democrat who is calling for a pause on data centre development is in a dead heat with a Republican who disagrees. Republican Senator John Husted of Ohio, who is fighting to keep his seat against Democrat Sherrod Brown, has also had to shift his position. Recent polls, external have found that the majority of Ohio voters oppose data centres. He has softened his support, saying that their arrival should be up to local citizens and elected officials. Meanwhile, Brown has stumped on his opposition to new data centres. He leads Husted in recent polls.Husted's trouble in Ohio led the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the major fundraising arm for conservatives in the Senate, to write in a private memo, external that Republican politicians needed to entirely reframe how they spoke to voters on data centres."This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle", the NRSC added.  Texas is perhaps the most clear cut example of how backlash has turned into an undeniable issue for even the most pro-business politician.The state currently has almost 300 operational data centres, with another 170 planned for development, according to Pew data.At the end of last year, Republican Governor Greg Abbott had boasted of Texas as "the epicentre of AI development" because of the number of data centres it housed. Within months he was backtracking, citing concerns of "safety and quality of life".It could play a part in the state's upcoming senate race too.Democrat James Talarico's campaign is pushing for an end to "sweetheart tax deals" for Big Tech. He's now seen as a frontrunner for the historically Republican seat, where he is facing off against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Paxton said in a late September interview that there was still "plenty of open space in Texas that we can put data centres".Many of the actions or proposals that have come from politicians looking to appease or address these voters are temporary. Most of the moratoriums, for instance, will end in one to three years.It is possible that the political winds will have shifted by the time such moratoriums expire, leaving Big Tech and AI firms to build as they wish.For now, people's feelings toward them are strong.Balaji Tammabattula, the chief executive of Barupon, is developing a roughly 700-acre data centre and technology campus in Liberty, Texas. Despite the buildings being designed to use rain capture for water and supply its own energy needs, an increasingly common design for major data centre projects, Tammabattula told the BBC that people in the community oppose the project out of hand."There's just such a high level of tension from the jump that you can't really even break through with the facts," he said.During a recent community event, Tammabattula said he tried to speak one-on-one with a woman who was vociferously opposed to the project. "She just looked right at me and said, 'Get the hell out of my state.'"

schema.headline: How data centres became the sleeper issue that could decide the US midterms

title: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
description: Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged.The PM dined
body: Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged.The PM dined with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches in 2017 and 2018 - but this was not detailed in a statement on Monday by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) about his meetings with the club.Burnham has been under pressure to clarify his previous discussions with Man City since the club was found guilty of having "systematically" broken Premier League rules, which it will appeal.The PM, who was mayor until June, sparked widespread controversy when he said last month he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners now sold up.Separately, it has emerged that a representative from the club joined a trade mission to India this week alongside Burnham's successor as mayor of Greater Manchester Bev Craig.The trade mission was organised by the business department, but as first reported in the Guardian,, external Manchester City's invitation came from the Great North, a coalition of Northern mayors and regional leaders. The government said it played no role in approving the club's presence on the trip. On Monday, the GMCA released a statement about Burnham's meetings with Man City in his role as mayor for the region for almost a decade.The statement said he had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade; and that he met the club chairman "informally in the stands" at a testimonial match in 2019 for former player Vincent Kompany.It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions".But the statement did not specify that this referred to, external two hospitality dinners he had with the Manchester City chairman at separate matches.A previous GMCA register of declarations for Burnham, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match at the Etihad stadium in August 2017, valued at £300 for hospitality.Below is another entry for "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately £699.Burnham previously declared those dinners, alongside a £150 pair of tickets to see Ed Sheeran perform at the stadium in May 2018.But the register of declarations has since been deleted from the GMCA website, as first reported by The Sun. The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term.BBC News has asked GMCA for more details about this policy - given its website has entries dating back to 2022, despite the current mayoral term beginning in 2024.Downing Street has defended the two dinners with Man City's chairman, saying this was hospitality received at home games, which had been declared, rather than separate meetings with the club chairman.But political pressure on Burnham to be clearer about any former discussions with Man City is continuing to mount.Tory shadow sports minister Louie French said: "Andy Burnham promised the country and House of Commons full transparency on his dealings with Manchester City."This was essential after his inappropriate intervention into football."And Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said "this saga stinks" as he accused Burnham of having apparently "concealed his extensive links to Man City's owners".Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded for several days that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.Burnham told the Rest Is Politics podcast last week he was "happy" to do this and would "quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester". "None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."Asked at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday whether anyone at the club had raised the charges they were facing with him or his team, Burnham said: "They did not raise those issues with me."With the PM continuing to face pressure on the issue, he told MPs he was happy for "everything to be set out in full", referring to the GMCA's statement as "a full statement of my key dealings with the owners of Manchester City Football Club".When asked by reporters why the statement did not refer to the two dinners, and what the difference is between "everything" and "key dealings", the PM's press secretary referred back to the GMCA statement.The list of meetings, which was published by the GMCA on Monday, did not include detail on what was discussed. The BBC has asked GMCA why the two dinners were not specifically mentioned.In September Man City - which has dominated the top flight of English football for years - was found guilty by an independent commission of breaching Premier League financial regulations.The commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations.Sanctions are yet to be announced and City, which denies any wrongdoing, has lodged an appeal against the verdict.Earlier this month, Sir Richard Leese - who was head of Manchester City Council for 25 years until 2021 - defended a decade-old deal between the council and Man City owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG).Under the partnership between the authority and the company, which is linked to the United Arab Emirates royal family, land was leased to ADUG at "below comparable rates", according to a University of Sheffield report.

schema.headline: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show

title: Fall in West Midlands gun crime down to policing and community efforts
description: More than 10 years ago, the West Midlands was dubbed the gun crime capital of England and Wales. It was an area suffering from high-profile shootings.
body: More than 10 years ago, the West Midlands was dubbed the gun crime capital of England and Wales. It was an area suffering from high-profile shootings. Gun fights between rival gangs were happening regularly.Figures at the time reflected that notoriety - there were more firearms offences per head in the West Midlands Police force area than anywhere else."Back then, there were shootings every day, reported shootings every day and unreported shootings every day," says Simeon Moore, also known as Zimbo, an ex-Johnson crew member - one of the Birmingham's most notorious gangs in the noughties.New figures seen by BBC News show shootings in the West Midlands force area - covering Birmingham, Wolverhampton, the Black Country and Coventry - have dropped significantly over the past six years."Things have calmed down dramatically since the early 2000s," Zimbo, who now mentors youngsters, said.While the numbers are not directly comparable, due to the criteria in the way they were gathered and published, in 2002-03 the force recorded about 1,300 gun crimes, external, compared with 504 in the 2024 calendar year, external.A more direct snapshot of the past six years also shows things are improving.In 2020-21, there were  a total of 157 firearms discharges, while a year later in 2021-2022 there were 148.By last year, the number of discharges had dropped to 69 and in the first seven months of 2026, there had only been 30, according to figures from West Midlands Police.The force said the fall was down to way it now dealt with firearms incidents. A major crime unit deals with all firearms events. Every time gun fire is reported, it is treated as if it was a murder.But it is not all down to policing, Zimbo said.He thinks there has been a change in culture, with more people speaking out about that kind of lifestyle, keeping the next generation out of trouble.He was jailed for six years for possessing a semi-automatic weapon as a teenager and was in and out of prison for two decades."We lived it," Zimbo said."There's more people that have been involved in that life talking about it, turning away from it and speaking bad about it in the sense that this isn't the right way to go."Now you've got man that have lived that life, done crazy sentences and they're telling the young people now, 'if you're going to start living like this, expect jail, expect to lose your friends or possibly lose your own life.'"At Revere Records in the city, where Zimbo heads up its urban division, a young artist, Solitary, is recording a track. His lyrics reference life in parts of the city, avoiding jail and being a product of your environment.This is just one of the projects Zimbo is involved with that gives youngsters opportunities. Zimbo added: "It's very hard for these young people to stay away from the lifestyle."West Midlands Police believes the reorganisation and creation of its major crime unit has led to the fall in gun crime, and a rise in seizures of weapons.Det Supt Ryan Chambers said the unit specialised in the most serious elements of criminality, targeting offenders and those in possession of firearms.He said 50% of the discharges the force dealt with were from shotguns which had been owned lawfully, but stolen in burglaries and ended up in criminal hands.Chambers said: "We've had a good level of success over the last 12-months. We've had the most recoveries and biggest reduction in discharges we've seen in recent years."

schema.headline: Fall in West Midlands gun crime down to policing and community efforts

title: I'm 12 and want to try protein powder - should I?
description: Twelve-year-old Ben is desperate to try protein powder but there's one hurdle: me, his mum. "I've asked about 20 times and you just keep saying no!",
body: Twelve-year-old Ben is desperate to try protein powder but there's one hurdle: me, his mum. "I've asked about 20 times and you just keep saying no!", he says, claiming it would make him "fitter and bigger" and that his male friends use it.In recent years, there's been an explosion of products marketed as "high protein", including milk, yoghurt, breads, cereals, bars and powders.Social media is flooded with adverts for various supplements, including protein powder. As a health journalist, I'm sceptical and think at Ben's age he must be getting enough protein through his diet.So, do experts think it's safe for pre-teens and teenagers or is a big, juicy steak just as good?For teenage boys and girls "you can get all the protein that you need from food alone", says registered dietitian Nichola Ludlam-Raine.It is important that teenage girls, especially, get enough iron and calcium, so Ludlam-Raine says not to become overly focused on protein at the expense of other nutrients.Protein shakes, powders or bars can be useful for some, including high-level athletes and those who have certain allergies, but they should not replace a healthy diet.There can also be some unwanted side effects from using protein powders such as bloating, gas, cramps, and diarrhoea.Those with pre-existing health conditions should not use it unless they have been told they can by their doctor.Ludlam-Raine points out that the protein powder market is not as tightly regulated as medicines."Of course, you can get reputable companies who do third-party testing and make sure that what you see on the label is what is in the inside, but that's not always the case," she says."And ultimately you can't just have a shake and your biceps grow."Some protein powders contain high amounts of added sugar, artificial ingredients, and hidden stimulants.Dr Ramnik Mathur is a consultant paediatrician from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Trust.He explains that we need micronutrients like zinc, calcium and magnesium, which are found in whole foods.So, if meals are replaced with protein shakes, those nutrients are lost.Experts suggest spreading out protein across the day and aiming for 20-25g per meal. If you're keen to up your intake, try some of these recipes.During puberty when children have growth spurts, they do need more protein because their body is growing rapidly, building new muscle and bone mass.But Mathur says there are risks to eating too much protein."If you look at social media, they'll say you need to eat a lot of protein, but your body can handle only so much."He explains that if you eat too much, it has to be excreted by the kidneys and liver which can become overloaded.Mathur explains: "We had a child here at the hospital where I work - he was taking so much protein that his kidneys just stopped working and he actually passed away."The key takeaway from Mathur: "If a 12-year-old child is eating a healthy balanced diet then they shouldn't need any more protein."Ludlam-Raine's advice is to get teens to improve their diet first before taking any protein powder, especially regularly.If they still want to use it, speak to a registered dietitian or nutritionist first.Now off I go to tell my son the answer is still no - and the experts say the same.

schema.headline: I'm 12 and want to try protein powder - should I?

title: World's oldest shipwreck found off Kekova Island in Turkey
description: Figure caption, Artefacts from the ship were found just off the coast of Kekova IslandByAlison FrancisRebecca Morelle and Kevin ChurchBBC News Science
body: Figure caption, Artefacts from the ship were found just off the coast of Kekova IslandByAlison FrancisRebecca Morelle and Kevin ChurchBBC News ScienceThe world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say.They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built.The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside.The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea."The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Öniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition.Image source, Hakan ÖnizImage caption, The divers found three stone anchors, as ships carried spares on long voyages The wreck is close to the shore of Kekova Island in Antalya, Turkey. The artefacts lie scattered across an underwater slope,  just 30m beneath the waves.Three large stone anchors were found, as well as more than 30 ceramic storage pots, called amphorae.The fact that none of the ship's wood remained meant techniques like radiocarbon dating - which measures a form of carbon in organic materials - could not be used to determine its age.Instead, archaeologists analysed the shape of the amphorae. Because pottery styles have changed over time, different styles are linked to particular periods.The Kekova ceramics are distinctive, with two handles, a ridge in the middle and a flat base.Öniz said this design matched other amphorae unearthed in Egypt and the Middle East that were known to be 4,400-4,700 years old."Comparing the decoration techniques… we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%."Image source, Hakan ÖnizImage caption, The amphorae were recovered and taken on board the research shipImage source, Hakan ÖnizImage caption, After thousands of years underwater, the fragile artefacts are now being carefully conservedDivers from the expedition brought the pots up to the surface, where they are now being carefully conserved after so many thousands of years underwater.Dr Karin Sowada, an archaeologist from Macquarie University, Australia, examined the amphorae after they were recovered. Some were intact and she was surprised to see they still contained a viscous, glossy residue."I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots…. a lot of this material was still remaining," she said.The team is now working to find out exactly what was being carried in the amphorae."It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins," Sowada said."It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years."The wreck and its cargo are also shedding light on trade in the ancient world.The archaeologists say the ship started its voyage from somewhere along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean.They believe it was taking goods to either the ancient city of Troy, in what is now north-western Turkey, or to the Minoan people in Crete.Image source, Hakan ÖnizImage caption, The divers worked underwater to carefully excavate the artefactsTravelling by sea was fraught with danger, particularly around Kekova Island, where the strong currents and winds have claimed many ships.There are hundreds of wrecks in the area, and the Mediterranean Archaeology Association specialises in finding and studying them.Öniz says that when he is diving on the wreck his first thoughts are about the lives of the people who were connected to this vessel."We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years."We are always thinking of the sailors... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back."The shipwreck is owned by the Turkish Ministry of Culture. Its minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said the artefacts that have been recovered would be put on display in the new Mediterranean Underwater Archaeology Museum in Antalya when it opens in the coming months.Image source, Hakan ÖnizImage caption, The depth meant the divers could only spend 30 minutes at a time exploring itThe Kekova discovery now tops the list of the world's oldest shipwrecks.Previously, the record holder was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, an island in southern Greece, which dates to about 4,200 years ago.The oldest known intact shipwreck, where the wood is still preserved, was found in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria. It dates to about 2,400 years ago.

schema.headline: World's oldest shipwreck found off Kekova Island in Turkey

title: I do not have confidence UK is safe from Russian threats - Swinney
description: Asked about the MI5 chief's comments, the first minister said he was "very worried" about a "lack of coastal and offshore protection". He identified w
body: Asked about the MI5 chief's comments, the first minister said he was "very worried" about a "lack of coastal and offshore protection". He identified waters north of Shetland as an area of significant Russian activity. "I don't think we've got nearly the presence in those areas that we require today," he told BBC Scotland News."There's an obligation on the United Kingdom government to make sure that the country is safe. And I don't think the defence posture of the United Kingdom enables me to have that confidence."Scotland is home to the UK's nuclear submarine fleet at Faslane, west of Glasgow. The SNP wants those weapons to be removed, but is in favour of an independent Scotland joining Nato. Swinney insisted that independence would not hamper Scotland's security, but rather give the country "more choices". The SNP leader said he had "always been a believer in defence co-operation between Scotland and other countries", citing Canada joining the EU's SAFE defence programme, external. Responding to the first minister's comments, a Ministry of Defence Spokesperson said:"The first duty of government is to keep its citizens safe, and this government is investing £298bn over the next four years to ensure we can tackle rising threats."The Navy is helping to patrol Nato's northern flank, with this year's carrier strike group deploying to the Arctic and the high north."To tackle these threats, we're also investing in new frigates for the Navy and high-tech uncrewed vessels as part of our Hybrid Navy, backed by £1.5bn in funding."Delivering a speech at the UN General Assembly, external last month, Burnham said his government would invest in defence and build up the UK's "hard power and deterrence". He added: "But we will not play Russia's game of trading escalatory rhetoric. Unlike Russia, we do not seek confrontation."

title: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
description: Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by petrol prices.Vehicle fuel prices jumped by
body: Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by petrol prices.Vehicle fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months.In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year.Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher. At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%.

schema.headline: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices

title: Russell Brand was a 'sexual predator', prosecution alleges as rape trial begins
description: The barrister said: "The circumstances of the offending were as wide and as varied as the defendant's career."She said that "regardless of who the wom
body: The barrister said: "The circumstances of the offending were as wide and as varied as the defendant's career."She said that "regardless of who the women were and what they said or did, Brand was not deterred"."His desire, strong desire, for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate and voracious," she told the court.The prosecutor told jurors that Brand would be "nice when he wanted to be, funny - undoubtedly - charming, likeable even, when he wanted something in return".But she said he would also be "demanding, entitled, a flirt with a huge sexual appetite - childlike in his expectation that his every desire should be met".The prosecutor said Brand would "appear indifferent, normal and untroubled by what had just occurred" after the encounters.She added that "sometimes he would leave promptly after the incident, sometimes making an excuse to get away, or sometimes simply continuing as though nothing wrong had happened".On Wednesday, the jury heard details of the alleged offences.The first complainant says she met Brand before he was famous in 1999, the jury was told.She had attended the Labour Party conference and went to a fringe event where she spoke to Brand. He later allegedly raped her.The prosecution said when Brand was questioned by police about this allegation of rape, "he said if it happened, he didn't remember the incident".He added that he did not remember the first complainant's name and that he "had never engaged in non-consensual activity".The second complainant worked for MTV at the time when she says Brand indecently assaulted her.She said Brand asked her where the toilets were and the woman offered to show him. When they reached the toilets, prosecutors say, Brand asked the woman to "come in" before grabbing her forearm.She resisted by struggling and pulling back. He had what she described as a desperate, wild-eyed look on his face, as he said: "Please please come in – oh go on."The third complainant says Brand orally raped her in a toilet after meeting her at a party in 2004.Within a minute of meeting, in the middle of a conversation, he lurched forward and grabbed her breasts and squeezed them with both hands, the jury was told.The prosecution said the woman remembered he had a "big, weird grin" on his face as he did so, then grabbed her arm and pulled her towards the toilets.The same woman said that as they were driving to another venue, Brand exposed himself, the court heard."He said, 'Come on, come on, suck it' – to which she just said, 'No no'," the prosecution added. "He simply laughed but appeared to accept her refusal."The fourth complainant says Brand pushed her up against a wall at Capital Radio in 2004 or 2005 and kissed her "sloppily and aggressively", and "grabbed her body, at her breasts, sides and buttocks, aggressively".She was able to push him away and he "just sniggered, like it was a joke", the prosecutor said.The jury then heard how the fifth complainant says she met Brand when he was performing at the Hammersmith Apollo in London in 2009.The prosecution said their encounter began with consensual activity, but that he raped her anally on a later occasion.The jury heard how the woman "spent months and years blaming herself", becoming anxious and unwell.They were told Brand texted the woman after seeing her at an event the following summer, saying: "I wanna push you further."She is said to have replied: "I think you pushed me far enough – you treated me like an animal." He allegedly replied: "I'm sorry."The sixth complainant - who has accused Brand of sexual assault - says he demanded a massage when she was on a work assignment in 2009.He "fell to his knees and placed his head directly into her groin area", the prosecution said.After the accounts of the final two women were heard, the prosecutor said Brand told police in 2023 "he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity, and that any accounts had been reinvented or imagined after a defamatory documentary and subsequent press reporting".On Wednesday afternoon, Brand's former flatmate Mark Pinheiro was the first witness to give evidence.Pinheiro told jurors that Brand had told him he may have gone a "bit too far" with a woman when visiting the Labour Party conference in 1999."He said that things got a little bit heated and a little bit out of hand, and he thinks that maybe he did go a little bit too far."Those were his words - 'I think I may have gone a bit too far'."Pinheiro was pressed under cross-examination about whether he accurately remembered the comment, but he told the court he was sure Brand had said "things may have gone a little bit too far" or "I may have taken things a little too far".The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.Brand was accompanied by his wife Laura to the court on Wednesday.He rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting and now lives in Florida in the United States.

title: Airport drop-off charges to be reviewed after sharp increase
description: Image source, Getty ImagesBySimon Browning Transport reporterAirport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price incre
body: Image source, Getty ImagesBySimon Browning Transport reporterAirport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price increases in recent years.Prices at major UK airports have risen by a third since the summer of 2025 on average, according to one analysis, with Gatwick and Stansted drop-off charges found to be the most expensive, jumping from £7 to £10.Such charges at Edinburgh Airport have risen from £6 to £8.50, while fees at Bournemouth increased from £5 to £8, the same price as Leeds Bradford and London City.The Department for Transport confirmed it had committed to a review, saying it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly".The government added it hoped airports would "exercise restraint on rises, particularly where there are limited public transport alternatives".'Rip-off' The RAC, which conducted the analysis in July this year, has campaigned against increases in drop-off charges. It said a review of "kiss and fly" fees would be "music to the ears to drivers"."We know airport drop-off charges are a growing source of anger and frustration," said Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC. "Four-in-five drivers we've surveyed believe they are a 'rip-off', with just one-in-10 understanding why airports charge what they do."The RAC's research found London City Airport, which only introduced charges in 2026, was the most expensive on a per-minute basis. Its £8 charge for five minutes works out at £1.60 per minute. Belfast International Airport now charges £5 for 10 minutes in the drop-off zone, up £2 on last year.None of the top 10 airports in the European Union charge for drop-offs, according to the RAC.It argues that international airports should not charge for dropping off passengers, however, the industry said the charges were a neccesary part of the business model of airports.Supporters of such charges also say they encourage travellers to use of more environmentally friendly modes of transport."Airports outside the UK are typically publicly owned and in receipt of state subsidies and tax exemptions, while UK airports are generally privately owned and subject to the full array of commercial rates of taxation," said Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, which represents airports.She added airports offered a "range of options for those travelling to terminals, including free drop off points" and that "any review" by the government would find airports make "excellent use of a variety of ways to manage traffic and air pollution".The Aviation Environment Federation campaign group has previously defended the fees, arguing they help reduce congestion and air pollution around airports.Earlier this month, the government announced extra charges for parents sitting with their children when flying would be scrapped in time for next year's summer holidays.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the changes were part of a series of "everyday fixes" to ease cost of living pressures on households.Get in touchHave you been affected by issues covered in this story?  Share your experiences.

title: Starlink: Musk says US government may be behind slowdown of Ukraine drone speeds
description: Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connecte
body: Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to SpaceX's Starlink internet network.Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said unexpected new speed limits were disrupting its battlefield missions.An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky said he believed the restrictions were not a coincidence and were related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.Musk said that Starshield, the military-grade sister service to Starlink, is controlled by the US government, and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".Musk - writing on X - had been responding to pleas from Ukrainian officials to restore connectivity, including from Zelensky who told UK media: "I hope that it's a mistake, maybe [a] huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to... switch [it] on."Starlink, which is owned by Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.It had been partially restored by Wednesday evening, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said."Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," he wrote on X, thanking Elon Musk and asking for his "continued support".About an hour later, Musk replied to that post, defending his company's involvement."Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.Musk added that Starlink is for "civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company".The US government has not commented.While both companies are owned by Musk's SpaceX, Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas, while Starshield is designed for government and military use.The restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that killed several people in Kyiv, officials said, and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military. Zelensky said it was "one of the largest attacks" from Russia, and while "a significant part of the drones were shot down" there were "also hits".At least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity, and residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit."It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.US President Donald Trump has grown increasingly frustrated towards Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities. Zelensky has said that the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire, but on Tuesday, Trump denied this.Speaking during a visit to London on Wednesday, Zelensky agreed that he had felt betrayed after the US made a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes of its diesel."Really yes... but it's a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings," Zelensky said, when asked by UK journalist Piers Morgan if he felt betrayed.During his one-day visit, Zelensky was greeted with a hug by UK PM Andy Burnham at Downing Street and held an audience with King Charles.Ahead of the president's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones."We are behind you and that will not change," Burnham told Zelensky.

schema.headline: Starlink: Musk says US government may be behind slowdown of Ukraine drone speeds

title: Dog that hunts invasive sea creature named animal of the year
description: "When I first started this project, I genuinely didn't know whether it would work," said Sim."No one had really explored whether dogs could help tackl
body: "When I first started this project, I genuinely didn't know whether it would work," said Sim."No one had really explored whether dogs could help tackle this problem in the marine environment. It began as a proof-of-concept project and has exceeded every expectation I had."Dogs' scent detection skills are often used in conservation work on land, including tracking endangered species and helping investigate environmental crime. At low tide, Sgiath can, as Sim puts it "dive down under the seaweed"."She just does a survey with her nose, essentially, she can pinpoint exactly where it is, so it's much easier," she said.Marine experts believe that carpet sea squirt, formally named Didemnum vexillum, came from Japan. It arrived on the shores of the south of England and Wales in 2008.It can appear in various shades - from orange to cream -  and has now spread to several seaside locations across the UK.It reproduces quickly during the warmer summer months and, with warming seas, there are fears it could spread further.Dr Martyn Kurr, a marine biologist from Bangor University told BBC News that non-native or "biofouling" species, like the carpet sea squirt, can outcompete native wildlife for valuable nutrients."These species also clog up aquaculture pens, marine infrastructure, and machinery such as boat propellors," he explained.Efforts to control and clean up these problematic marine invaders costs millions of pounds every year across Europe.

schema.headline: Dog that hunts invasive sea creature named animal of the year

title: Ukraine war: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield?
description: Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air f
body: Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.Barros, who is the ISW's Director of Innovation and Open Source Tradecraft told the BBC that the restrictions could have major implications as the technology allows "drones, artillery and command posts to function as a single real-time network where the time between sensor-to-shooter is minimized."Starlink does not work inside Russia, but Ukrainian drones can use the satellites to communicate back to their operators during strikes. There is no ready replacement for the network.Starlink-enabled interceptors are also among Ukraine's most effective solution against jet-powered Russian Shahed drones, he said.Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph, meaning SpaceX's restriction makes Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.Tom Whittington, electronic warfare expert and associate fellow at RUSI, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the satellite system allows Ukraine to move large amounts of data - like video, text and voice calls - in a similar way that smartphones do but without the infrastructure that phones need.The speed restrictions "effectively preclude" anything connected to the network going above 100mph, Whittington said, making drone navigation difficult within Ukraine and Russian-occupied territory inside Ukraine.Serhiy Beskrestnov - Zelensky's adviser - says he believes the restrictions are not a coincidence and are related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.US President Donald Trump has criticised Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and called for a new leader - criticisms which have been echoed by Elon Musk.Ukraine's complaint about the restrictions has drawn attention to both Starlink, and  Starshield - a military-grade version of the network developed for the Pentagon by SpaceX.Musk says the two systems are separate, but in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.And in a post on X, external, Musk suggested the US government could be responsible for the slowdown afflicting Ukrainian usage of the technology."Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.SpaceX's satellite communications have proved vital to both armies during the four-year war, including a Russian attack on a moving passenger train, but earlier this year Musk cut the use of Starlink terminals for Russian forces in a move that blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders.

schema.headline: Ukraine war: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield?
